title: Fragments, run-ons and comma splices
blurb: Spot an incomplete sentence or two sentences jammed together, and fix it with one of the five correct joins.
question: A care note reads, “The patient walked twice today, however she needed help on the stairs. Because her knee was stiff.” What two sentence errors are here, and which revision fixes both?

teach.body: Formally, a complete sentence has a subject, a verb and a complete thought. A fragment lacks one of these. A run-on (fused sentence) joins two independent clauses with no punctuation; a comma splice joins them with only a comma. Plain English: a fragment is too little to stand alone, and run-ons and comma splices are too much crammed into one sentence without a proper join. Length has nothing to do with it.

rows.label: Example
values: The bus was late we missed it.
The bus was late, we missed it.

rows.label: Quick fix
values: Attach it or add the missing part

children.label: Fragment
children.sub: Missing subject, verb, or starts with because/when/who

teach.caption: Imperatives are complete: “Wash your hands.” has an implied subject, you.

teach.h: Five correct ways to join two clauses
head: Fix
Example
rows: The bus was late. We missed it.
The bus was late; we missed it.
The bus was late, so we missed it.
The bus was late; therefore, we missed it.
Because the bus was late, we missed it.
teach.caption: A comma alone, or a comma before however, therefore or then, is never enough.

rows.label: Correct
values: She was tired, but she stayed.
She was tired; however, she stayed.

rows.label: Splice
values: She was tired, however, she stayed.

teach.caption: Same for therefore, moreover, consequently, nevertheless and thus.

rows.label: Running to the clinic before dawn.

teach.note: “The nurse who works nights” has a verb, but it belongs to the dependent clause “who works nights”; the subject “The nurse” has no verb of its own.

teach.h: Scenario: Destiny fixes the care note
teach.body: Destiny Carter, a nursing applicant, spots two errors. “...today, however she needed help” is a comma splice: however cannot join clauses with a comma. “Because her knee was stiff.” is a fragment: a dependent clause alone. Her revision: “The patient walked twice today; however, she needed help on the stairs because her knee was stiff.” The semicolon fixes the splice, and attaching the because-clause fixes the fragment.

A related structure error: the subject and predicate do not fit logically. “The reason is because...” repeats the idea of cause; write “The reason is that...”. “Hypertension is when...” defines a condition as a time; write “Hypertension is a condition in which...”. On the TEAS, the correct option names a thing with a noun after “is.”

teach.text: TEAS traps: treating “however” like “but” (a comma splice), assuming a long sentence is a run-on (count clauses, not words), calling a short imperative a fragment, and accepting a fix that swaps one error for another, such as a semicolon before a dependent clause.

items: Fragment: missing subject, verb or complete thought; a dependent clause alone is a fragment.
Run-on: two independent clauses with no punctuation. Comma splice: joined by a comma only.
Five fixes: period; semicolon; comma + FANBOYS; semicolon + conjunctive adverb + comma; subordination.
However, therefore and then cannot join clauses with just a comma.
Write “the reason is that,” not “the reason is because.”

summary: You can now identify fragments, run-ons and comma splices by counting independent clauses, and repair them with the five correct joins. You can also avoid the traps of however-splices, long-but-correct sentences and faulty predication.

A.q: Which of the following is a complete sentence?
options: Because the shift ran late.
Running to the clinic before dawn.
The nurse who works nights.
Wash your hands before entering.
A.why: An imperative has an implied subject (you) and a verb (wash), so it is complete.

whyNot.0: “Because” makes this a dependent clause standing alone: a fragment.
whyNot.1: This participial phrase has no subject and no main verb: a fragment.
whyNot.2: “Who works nights” describes the nurse, but “The nurse” has no main verb: a fragment.

A.q: Which of the following is a comma splice?
options: The bus was late, so we missed the appointment.
The bus was late, we missed the appointment.
The bus was late; we missed the appointment.
Because the bus was late, we missed the appointment.
A.why: Two independent clauses are joined by a comma alone.

whyNot.0: A comma plus the coordinating conjunction “so” is a correct join.
whyNot.2: A semicolon correctly joins two independent clauses.
whyNot.3: “Because the bus was late” is dependent, so the comma after it is correct.

A.q: Which revision correctly fixes this run-on? “The pharmacy closed early we drove to another one.”
options: The pharmacy closed early, so we drove to another one.
The pharmacy closed early, we drove to another one.
The pharmacy closed early so, we drove to another one.
The pharmacy closed early, therefore we drove to another one.
A.why: A comma before the coordinating conjunction “so” correctly joins two independent clauses.

whyNot.1: A comma alone turns the run-on into a comma splice.
whyNot.2: The comma belongs before “so,” not after it.
whyNot.3: “Therefore” is a conjunctive adverb, so a comma before it still leaves a comma splice.

B.q: Which sentence about the long test is punctuated correctly?
options: The test was long, however, Ana finished early.
The test was long however, Ana finished early.
The test was long; however, Ana finished early.
The test was long, however Ana finished early.
B.why: “However” joining two independent clauses needs a semicolon before it and a comma after it.

whyNot.0: Commas around “however” still leave a comma splice.
whyNot.1: With no mark before “however,” the clauses are fused.
whyNot.3: A comma alone before “however” is a comma splice.

B.q: Which of the following is a sentence fragment?
options: Smiling, the nurse greeted the family.
The family arrived after visiting hours.
Please stay with your father tonight.
The doctor who ordered the new tests.
B.why: “Who ordered the new tests” is a dependent clause describing the doctor; the subject “The doctor” has no main verb.

whyNot.0: “The nurse greeted the family” is a complete clause; “Smiling” is just an introductory word.
whyNot.1: It has a subject (family), verb (arrived) and complete thought.
whyNot.2: An imperative with the implied subject “you” is complete.

options: The reason she was late is because the bus broke down.
The reason she was late is that the bus broke down.
Hypertension is when blood pressure stays too high.
Tardiness is when a student arrives after class starts.
B.why: “The reason ... is that” correctly links the subject “reason” to a noun clause.

whyNot.0: “The reason is because” repeats the idea of cause; use “that.”
whyNot.2: A condition is not a time; write “a condition in which.”
whyNot.3: Tardiness is not a time; “is when” is faulty predication.

C.q: Which sentence is correctly punctuated and is NOT a run-on or comma splice?
options: Although the clinic was very busy that morning, the nurses stayed calm and kept everyone informed.
The clinic was very busy that morning, the nurses stayed calm and kept everyone informed.
The clinic was very busy that morning the nurses stayed calm and kept everyone informed.
The clinic was very busy that morning, however, the nurses stayed calm and kept everyone informed.
C.why: It has one dependent clause and one independent clause joined correctly by a comma. It is long but not a run-on.

whyNot.1: Two independent clauses joined by only a comma: a comma splice.
whyNot.2: Two independent clauses with no punctuation: a run-on.
whyNot.3: “However” between commas cannot join two independent clauses: a comma splice.

C.q: Destiny's care plan says, “Mr. Okafor walked twice today. Without assistance.” Which revision corrects the fragment?
options: Mr. Okafor walked twice today, without, assistance.
Mr. Okafor walked twice today; without assistance.
Mr. Okafor walked twice today without assistance.
Mr. Okafor walked twice today. Without any assistance.
C.why: Attaching the prepositional phrase to the independent clause makes one complete sentence.

whyNot.0: The comma after “without” splits the preposition from its object.
whyNot.1: A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, not a phrase.
whyNot.3: “Without any assistance” is still a fragment standing alone.

C.q: Which revision of “The patient felt better, she still needed rest” fixes the comma splice and keeps the contrast?
options: Because the patient felt better, she still needed rest.
The patient felt better, and she still needed rest.
The patient felt better; therefore, she still needed rest.
Although the patient felt better, she still needed rest.
C.why: “Although” signals contrast and makes the first clause dependent, which fixes the splice.

whyNot.0: “Because” signals cause, which makes no sense: feeling better is not why she needed rest.
whyNot.1: “And” signals addition, not contrast, so the meaning changes.
whyNot.2: “Therefore” signals a result, not a contrast.

reteach.title: Sentences are train couplings
reteach.question: Picture each independent clause as a train car with its own engine. What happens if you hook two together with no coupling, or with a coupling that is too weak?

blocks.body: Two engine cars with no coupling crash into each other: a run-on. A comma is a coupling made of string: it snaps (a comma splice). Strong couplings are a period (separate trains), a semicolon, a comma plus FANBOYS, or a semicolon plus however and a comma. A fragment is a single trailer with no engine: it cannot move until you hook it to an engine car.

blocks.text: A long train with one engine and several trailers is fine. Length never makes a sentence a run-on.

explain.body: A fragment is missing a subject, a main verb, or a complete thought. A dependent clause (Although she left early.) is a fragment even though it has a subject and verb. Commands are not fragments.

test.q: Which word group is a fragment?
options: She left.
Although she left early.
Leave now.
She left early, but I stayed.
test.why: “Although” makes the clause dependent, so it cannot stand alone.

whyNot.0: A subject and a verb with a complete thought: a sentence.
whyNot.2: An imperative with the implied subject “you”: a sentence.
whyNot.3: Two independent clauses correctly joined by a comma and “but.”

explain.body: A run-on (fused sentence) puts two independent clauses side by side with no punctuation. A comma splice joins them with a comma alone.

test.q: How is this sentence best described? “The lab results came back the doctor called the patient.”
options: A fused (run-on) sentence
A comma splice
A sentence fragment
A correct compound sentence
test.why: Two independent clauses (results came back; doctor called) sit together with no punctuation: a fused sentence.

whyNot.1: A comma splice has a comma between the clauses; this has none.
whyNot.2: Both clauses have subjects and verbs, so nothing is missing.
whyNot.3: A compound sentence needs a comma + FANBOYS or a semicolon.

explain.body: Fix a run-on or splice with a period, a semicolon, a comma + FANBOYS, a semicolon + conjunctive adverb + comma, or by making one clause dependent. A comma + then is not a fix: then is not a coordinating conjunction.

test.q: Which is NOT a correct way to fix “The power failed, the generator started”?
options: The power failed. The generator started.
The power failed; the generator started.
The power failed, then the generator started.
When the power failed, the generator started.
test.why: “Then” is an adverb, not a coordinating conjunction, so a comma before it still leaves a comma splice.

whyNot.0: A period makes two correct sentences.
whyNot.1: A semicolon correctly joins two independent clauses.
whyNot.3: Making the first clause dependent with “When” is a correct fix.

explain.body: But is a coordinating conjunction: a comma before it joins two clauses. However is a conjunctive adverb: it needs a semicolon before it and a comma after it when it joins clauses.

test.q: Which sentence uses however correctly between two clauses?
options: Jo studied hard, however, the exam was tough.
Jo studied hard however; the exam was tough.
Jo studied hard, however the exam was tough.
Jo studied hard; however, the exam was tough.
test.why: A semicolon before “however” and a comma after it correctly join the two independent clauses.

whyNot.0: Commas around “however” leave a comma splice.
whyNot.1: The semicolon must come before “however,” not after it.
whyNot.2: A comma alone before “however” is a comma splice.
